title: Liners, bases & luting cements
blurb: Calcium hydroxide, zinc oxide eugenol, zinc phosphate, polycarboxylate, glass ionomer and resin cements: what each does, and how to mix it well.
question: The dentist is fitting a metal crown and asks you to mix zinc phosphate cement. Last time, the mix got warm and set before the crown was seated. What should you do differently, and what property does the cement need so the crown seats fully?

teach.body: Dental cements do three main jobs. A liner is a thin layer placed on the deepest part of a cavity to protect the pulp. A base is a thicker layer that replaces lost dentine, insulates the pulp from heat and cold, and supports the filling above it. A luting cement is a thin film that fixes (cements) a crown, bridge, inlay, veneer or post in place. Some cements can do more than one job, depending on how thickly they are mixed.

teach.caption: Decay that runs deep into dentine leaves only a thin layer of dentine over the pulp. Once the decay is removed, a liner goes on the floor nearest the pulp, a base fills out the lost dentine, and the restoration sits on top.

teach.h: Layers in a deep cavity, top to bottom

steps.label: Restoration
steps.sub: Amalgam or composite: takes the biting load

steps.label: Base
steps.sub: Thick layer: insulates and supports (e.g. GIC)

steps.label: Liner
steps.sub: Thin layer: protects the pulp (e.g. calcium hydroxide)

teach.body: Calcium hydroxide is strongly alkaline. This kills bacteria and encourages the pulp to lay down new reparative (tertiary) dentine, so it is used as a liner in very deep cavities and for pulp capping. It is weak and dissolves easily, so it is always covered with a base. The common two-paste type is dispensed as equal amounts of base and catalyst on a paper pad and mixed with a small ball-ended applicator, which is also used to place it. Light-cured versions exist too.

head: Cement
Mix on
Main uses
Watch out
rows: Gives off heat; acidic at first
teach.caption: Polycarboxylate and glass ionomer bond chemically to tooth. Zinc phosphate relies purely on mechanical retention.

teach.body: Zinc phosphate is a zinc oxide powder mixed with a phosphoric acid liquid. The setting reaction gives off heat (it is exothermic), and heat speeds up setting. So it is mixed on a cool, dry glass slab, adding the powder in small portions and spreading the mix over a wide area of the slab to lose heat. This lengthens the working time and lets more powder be added for strength. Any water on the slab upsets the powder:liquid ratio and shortens working time.

items: Cool and thoroughly dry the glass slab; have a stainless steel spatula ready.
Dispense powder and liquid as the manufacturer directs; replace the bottle caps.
Divide the powder into small portions and add them to the liquid one at a time.
Spatulate over a wide area of the slab to dissipate heat.
Stop when the mix is smooth and creamy, then line the crown thinly as the dentist directs.

teach.h: Zinc oxide eugenol, and the eugenol problem
teach.body: Zinc oxide eugenol (ZOE) smells of cloves. Eugenol soothes an inflamed pulp (it is obtundent) and is antibacterial, so ZOE is used for sedative dressings, temporary fillings and temporary crown cement. But eugenol stops resin materials from setting properly. It must never go under composite, and before bonded or resin-cemented work, any ZOE residue is removed and a non-eugenol temporary cement is used instead.

teach.text: Luting cement must spread into a very THIN film (low film thickness). A thick mix stops the crown seating fully, leaving it high in the bite with an open margin.

items: Liner = thin, protects pulp; base = thick, insulates and supports; luting = thin film to fix restorations.
Calcium hydroxide: alkaline, antibacterial, stimulates reparative dentine; weak, so cover it.
Zinc phosphate: cool dry glass slab, small powder portions, wide spatulation.
ZOE soothes the pulp, but eugenol inhibits resin setting.
Polycarboxylate and GIC bond chemically; resin cements need etch and bond.

summary: You can now tell liners, bases and luting cements apart, explain where each sits in a deep cavity, describe calcium hydroxide, zinc oxide eugenol, zinc phosphate, polycarboxylate, glass ionomer and resin cements, mix zinc phosphate correctly on a cool slab, and avoid the eugenol and film-thickness traps.

A.q: A zinc phosphate mix becomes warm and sets too quickly. What should you do next time?
options: Add a drop of water to cool the mix
Add all of the powder in one go
Use a cool slab; add powder in portions
Mix it on a paper pad instead of glass
A.why: The reaction gives off heat. A cool, dry slab and small powder portions spread widely dissipate heat and lengthen working time.

whyNot.0: Water upsets the powder:liquid ratio and spoils the cement.
whyNot.1: Adding all the powder at once makes the mix hotter and faster setting.
whyNot.3: A paper pad can't absorb heat like a cool glass slab can.

A.q: A tooth with a ZOE temporary is to receive a bonded composite today. What is the most important precaution?
options: Leave the ZOE residue to help bonding
Etch straight over the ZOE residue
Use a longer curing time only
A.why: Eugenol inhibits resin setting, so all residue must be removed before bonding. Non-eugenol temporaries are preferred before bonded work.

whyNot.0: Eugenol residue weakens the bond rather than helping it.
whyNot.1: Etching doesn't reliably remove eugenol contamination.
whyNot.3: Longer curing won't overcome eugenol's effect on resin.

A.q: Why is calcium hydroxide placed as a liner in a very deep cavity?
options: It gives the filling its strength
It bonds the filling to enamel
It releases large amounts of fluoride
A.why: Its high alkalinity is antibacterial and encourages the pulp to lay down reparative (tertiary) dentine.

whyNot.1: Calcium hydroxide is weak; it needs a base and restoration over it.
whyNot.2: It doesn't bond the filling to enamel; that's the job of etch and bond.
whyNot.3: Fluoride release is a property of glass ionomer.

B.q: A luting cement is chosen because it spreads into a very thin layer under a crown. Which property is this?
B.why: Low film thickness lets the crown seat fully, so it isn't high in the bite and the margin is closed.

whyNot.0: Strength matters, but it doesn't describe how thinly the cement spreads.
whyNot.1: Conductivity is about heat transfer, which is undesirable in a cement.
whyNot.2: Translucency is an aesthetic property, mainly relevant to resin cements under veneers.

B.q: The glass slab still has water on it when you start mixing a cement. Why is this a problem?
options: It makes the cement more radiopaque
It gives a longer working time
B.why: Extra water alters the intended ratio, changing how the cement handles, sets and performs.

whyNot.0: Water doesn't make a cement show up more on radiographs.
whyNot.2: Water usually speeds setting and shortens working time.
whyNot.3: Water doesn't improve film thickness; it spoils the mix.

B.q: Which cement bonds chemically to tooth and is made from zinc oxide powder and polyacrylic acid?
B.why: Zinc polycarboxylate combines zinc oxide with polyacrylic acid, which bonds chemically to tooth.

whyNot.0: Zinc phosphate uses phosphoric acid and has no chemical bond to tooth.
whyNot.2: ZOE uses eugenol liquid and doesn't bond chemically.
whyNot.3: Calcium hydroxide is a two-paste liner, not a zinc-based cement.

C.q: The dentist is cementing a porcelain veneer. Which cement is most likely to be used?
C.why: Resin cements are strong, tooth-coloured and bond to etched tooth and treated ceramic, making them the choice for veneers.

whyNot.0: ZOE is temporary and its eugenol would stop resin bonding.
whyNot.1: Zinc phosphate is opaque and doesn't bond, so it isn't used for veneers.
whyNot.2: Calcium hydroxide is a liner, not a luting cement.

C.q: What is the main difference between a liner and a base?
options: A liner is thin; a base is thicker
A liner is permanent; a base is not
A liner goes over the filling
A base is only used under crowns
C.why: A liner is a thin protective layer on the deepest part of the cavity; a base is thicker, replacing dentine and giving insulation and support.

whyNot.1: Both stay in place under the permanent restoration.
whyNot.2: Liners go under the filling, on the cavity floor.
whyNot.3: Bases are used under fillings, not just crowns.

C.q: Why should calcium hydroxide always be covered by a base or restoration?
options: It sets too hard to carve
It is weak and dissolves easily
It is acidic and irritates the pulp
C.why: Calcium hydroxide has low strength and is soluble, so it must be protected by a stronger layer.

whyNot.0: Calcium hydroxide is soft, not too hard.
whyNot.3: Calcium hydroxide is alkaline and protects the pulp rather than irritating it.

reteach.title: Think of building a floor
reteach.question: Laying a new floor over a damaged one, you add a protective layer, then levelling screed, then the tiles. How does that match a deep filling?

blocks.body: First a thin damp-proof layer protects what's underneath: that's the liner, protecting the pulp. Next, thick screed fills the dips and gives a firm, insulated surface: that's the base, replacing lost dentine. Then the tiles go on top to take the wear: that's the amalgam or composite. Luting cement is different: it's like tile adhesive, a thin film whose job is to hold something already made, such as a crown, firmly in place.

blocks.text: Tile adhesive applied too thickly stops the tile sitting flat. Luting cement mixed too thick stops the crown seating fully.

explain.body: A liner is a thin layer on the cavity floor nearest the pulp, such as calcium hydroxide or a GIC liner. A base is a thicker layer that replaces lost dentine, insulates and supports the restoration.

explain.caption: Deep decay leaves little dentine over the pulp. After the decay is removed: liner nearest the pulp, base above it, restoration on top.

test.q: Which layer sits closest to the pulp in a deep restoration?
test.why: The liner is placed on the deepest part of the cavity, nearest the pulp.

whyNot.0: The base sits on top of the liner.
whyNot.2: The restoration is the top layer.
whyNot.3: Luting cement fixes indirect restorations; it isn't a cavity layer under a filling.

explain.body: Zinc oxide powder plus phosphoric acid. Its setting reaction gives off heat, so mix on a cool, dry glass slab, adding small portions of powder and spreading widely. It is used for luting crowns and as a base, and relies on mechanical retention.

test.q: Why is zinc phosphate mixed on a cool glass slab?
options: To absorb heat and extend working time
To make the mix more translucent
To stop the cement sticking to the slab
To add a little moisture to the mix
test.why: The setting reaction is exothermic; a cool slab absorbs the heat and slows setting.

whyNot.1: The slab's temperature doesn't change the cement's translucency.
whyNot.2: The slab isn't chosen to stop sticking; it's chosen to absorb heat.
whyNot.3: The slab must be dry; moisture spoils the mix.

explain.body: ZOE soothes the pulp and is antibacterial, so it is used for sedative dressings, temporary fillings and temporary crown cement. Eugenol inhibits resin setting, so never use it under composite and remove residue before bonded work.

test.q: Why is zinc oxide eugenol avoided under composite restorations?
options: It is too strong to remove
It conducts heat to the pulp
test.why: Eugenol interferes with the polymerisation of resin materials, weakening the composite and its bond.

whyNot.2: ZOE is a relatively weak, removable material.
whyNot.3: ZOE is a poor conductor of heat; that isn't the problem.

explain.body: Luting cements need low film thickness so restorations seat fully, plus low solubility and enough working time. Resin cements are strong, tooth-coloured and insoluble, used for veneers, ceramics and fibre posts, but need etching and bonding.

test.q: What problem is caused by a luting cement mixed too thick?
test.why: A thick cement film holds the crown up, leaving it high in the bite with an open margin.

whyNot.1: Cement thickness doesn't change the crown's colour.
whyNot.2: Only eugenol-containing cements release eugenol, regardless of thickness.
whyNot.3: Cement thickness doesn't make the tooth radiolucent.
